subject: Chemistry
title: Why Deodorant Stops Smell
description: A fast breakdown of Why Deodorant Stops Smell for builders.

hook.text: Sweat is odorless. The smell comes from bacteria on your skin breaking down sweat into stinky acids.

buildup.text: Apocrine glands in armpits produce protein-rich sweat. Bacteria feast on it and release thioalcohols.

discovery.text: Deodorants use antimicrobials to kill bacteria. Antiperspirants use aluminum salts to block sweat glands.

twist.text: Aluminum chloride forms a gel plug inside sweat ducts, physically preventing sweat from reaching the surface.

climax.text: Fragrance masks remaining odor. It's a three-layer chemical defense: kill, block, and cover.

punchline.text: Kill the bacteria, block the sweat, mask the rest. Chemistry vs. body odor.

quiz.question: What actually causes body odor?
options: Bacteria on skin breaking down sweat into acids
Sweat itself has a strong natural smell
Dead skin cells decomposing on the surface

details.summary: Body odor is produced when bacteria on the skin metabolize proteins and fatty acids in sweat into volatile sulfur and carboxylic acid compounds..
details.whyItMatters: Deodorant science combines microbiology, organic chemistry, and materials science. The distinction between deodorants and antiperspirants reveals different chemical strategies for the same problem.
takeaways: Sweat itself is nearly odorless; bacteria produce the smell
Antiperspirants use aluminum salts to form gel plugs in sweat ducts
Deodorants target bacteria rather than blocking sweat production

faq.question: Why does fresh sweat not smell but old sweat does?
faq.answer: Sweat from eccrine glands is mostly water and salt with minimal odor. Apocrine glands in armpits release protein-rich secretions that bacteria find nutritious. It takes time for bacteria to break down these proteins into thioalcohols and volatile acids that produce the characteristic body odor.

faq.question: Are aluminum salts in antiperspirants harmful to health?
faq.answer: Major health organizations including the FDA and WHO have found no conclusive evidence linking aluminum in antiperspirants to breast cancer or Alzheimer's disease. The small amounts absorbed through skin are efficiently excreted by the kidneys..
